clips.text_zh: Condo困局認真共鳴。22歲靠狗狗幣賺一筆，兩年唔返工去旅行，230K 買咗個Condo。之後錢燒晒，去讀返書畢業，依家返緊100K份工，27歲又再返去返工、消費、重複。學生貸款、信用卡債全部壓住。佢嗰句『食過好日子就返唔到去』真係頂我肺。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: I made random crypto money from dogecoin at 22. I lived two years on perma vacation, dropped out of school and bought a condo for $230K. Then the money ran out. I went back, graduated, and earn $100K now at 27. I hate that I got a taste of the rich life and cannot go back.
clips.source_hint: Anon rants about early crypto gains trapping him in condo debt cycle

signal.rationale: Pure life-story post about crypto gains gone wrong, no actionable setup

clips.text_en_b2: I struck it rich with dogecoin at 22, so I dropped out, blew two years travelling, and splashed out $230K on a condo. The money eventually dried up, forcing me back to school and into a $100K job by 27. What really gets under my skin is that having tasted the easy life, I can't stomach going back to the grind, even while student loans and credit card debt pile up.
clips.text_en_c1: Striking how thoroughly this resonates. I stumbled into a windfall from dogecoin at 22, promptly abandoned my studies, and proceeded to blow the better part of two years globe-trotting on what felt like a permanent holiday. Somewhere along the way I sank $230K into a condo, convinced the gravy train would never end. It did. I crawled back, eventually graduated, and now at 27 I'm back to grinding out a $100K salary, shackled to student loans and a stack of credit card debt. What genuinely haunts me is having sampled genuine leisure and knowing full well I can't reclaim it. Work, spend, repeat — the hamster wheel resumes.
clips.text_en_c2: At twenty-two I stumbled into an improbable windfall from dogecoin, a stroke of fortune that effectively derailed any conventional life trajectory. For two years I drifted through what was essentially permanent leisure, deferring my education while sinking $230K into a condominium I could ill afford once the euphoria faded. Eventually the capital evaporated; I returned to university, graduated, and now draw a $100K salary at twenty-seven, shackled to student loans and revolving credit card debt. The cruel irony is that having tasted unfettered abundance, the gravitational pull back to the work-consume-repay cycle feels almost unbearable. One adjusts, ostensibly, yet the memory of that prior freedom renders every spreadsheet an exercise in quiet resignation. You adapt, but you never truly reconcile.

clips.text_zh: 成日都係咁。BTC 悶幾個星期冇人理，pump 15% 之後個個湧入。問吓點解唔喺橫行嗰陣入場啦，唔好又係FOMO追頂啦🙏 永遠都係郁完先知，等到喊都冇用。
clips.text_en_b1: Why do people buy BTC after the pump? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Why does everyone want to buy after the move already happened? This pattern repeats every single cycle and people still fall for it.
clips.source_hint: Anon calls out retail buying BTC after the move

signal.rationale: Post is observational critique of FOMO behaviour, no clear long or short setup

clips.text_en_b2: This is getting ridiculous. BTC consolidates for weeks on end, nobody bats an eye, then a 15% pump suddenly pulls the crowd back in. People who refuse to build positions during the sideways action pile in afterwards because FOMO kicks in. The pattern plays out every cycle, yet retail traders keep falling for the same trap and end up buying the top.
clips.text_en_c1: The cycle never fails to repeat itself. BTC will consolidate sideways for weeks on end, met with total indifference from the broader market, and then the moment it rips 15% higher, the FOMO crowd materialises out of thin air demanding entry. What I genuinely cannot fathom is why anyone would chase momentum after the move has already played out, yet every single cycle without exception, retail capitulates into positions at or near the local top. By the time the chorus of regret kicks in, the liquidation cascade has typically already begun. It's almost poetic in its predictability.
clips.text_en_c2: The phenomenon is almost mechanical in its predictability: Bitcoin languishes in prolonged consolidation for weeks on end, commanding scarcely a glance from retail participants, before suddenly vaulting fifteen percent in a matter of days. At that precise moment, an army of opportunistic latecomers materialises, scrambling to establish positions at precisely the wrong juncture. The question scarcely needs asking, yet it bears repeating: why does the buying impulse only crystallise after the substantive price discovery has already occurred? This behavioural pattern, wherein investors capitulate to fear of missing out precisely when asymmetric upside has been exhausted, recurs with metronomic regularity across every cycle. The chorus of lamentation that subsequently arises is therefore entirely self-inflicted, a ritual the market performs with wearying inevitability. History, it seems, offers instruction to precisely no one.

clips.text_zh: OpenAI 9月8號宣稱個 Astra 模型（用GPT-6）解咗個難題，燒咗2000萬美金計力。但研究員 Tristan Buckmaster 指出，佢自己用 OpenAI 自己嘅 Codex 加 Anthropic 嘅 Claude 做嘅研究同 Astra 嘅做法好相似。AI 咁樣食人研究成果，仲有冇人想繼續做研究？wtf。
clips.text_en_b1: On September 8th OpenAI claimed their Astra model, built on GPT-6, solved a big research problem using about $20 million in compute. Researcher Tristan Buckmaster then pointed out that OpenAI's approach closely matches his own independent work, which he had been refining with OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude. The video alleges serious ethical conflict around AI models stealing or copying human research.
clips.source_hint: Anon posts about OpenAI allegedly cribbing a researcher's work for GPT-6 Astra

signal.rationale: Tech ethics drama, not a trade

clips.text_en_b2: On September 8th, OpenAI claimed their Astra model, which runs on GPT-6, cracked a major research problem while burning through roughly $20 million in compute. Then researcher Tristan Buckmaster pointed out that OpenAI's methodology closely resembles his own independent work, refined using OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude. The whole saga raises uncomfortable questions about AI systems quietly absorbing human research without proper credit.
clips.text_en_c1: On September 8th, OpenAI announced that their Astra model, ostensibly built atop GPT-6, had cracked a significant research problem at an estimated compute cost of roughly $20 million. Independent researcher Tristan Buckmaster subsequently drew attention to the uncomfortable fact that his own work, developed iteratively using OpenAI's own Codex alongside Anthropic's Claude, bears striking methodological similarities to what Astra claims to have achieved. If frontier models are systematically absorbing, repackaging, and republishing the intellectual labour of the very researchers whose tools built them, one has to ask whether academic contribution to this ecosystem remains remotely rational.
clips.text_en_c2: On the eighth of September, OpenAI made the rather audacious claim that its Astra model, constructed atop the GPT-6 architecture, had resolved a formidable research problem at an expenditure of roughly twenty million dollars in compute resources. The triumphalist narrative, however, swiftly unravelled when the independent researcher Tristan Buckmaster publicly observed that Astra's methodology bore a striking resemblance to his own ongoing investigations, work he had been painstakingly refining through an iterative dialogue with OpenAI's own Codex alongside Anthropic's Claude. The implications are profoundly disquieting: if frontier AI systems can effectively ingest, digest, and repurpose human intellectual labour without attribution or compensation, what rational incentive remains for researchers to publish, share, or even pursue open inquiry? The entire apparatus of collaborative science risks being hollowed out from within, a grotesque inversion of the ecosystem that…

clips.text_zh: 新 OECD PISA 報告，91個國家76萬學生，全球數學同閱讀分數全部插水。但中國學生一枝獨秀，數學頂級Level 5要607分，中國平均612分。香港細路讀書真係俾人遠遠拋開。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: New OECD PISA study covered 760,000 students across 91 countries. Global math and reading scores are cratering and kids are getting dumber everywhere, except in China. Chinese students are the smartest by a huge margin. Level 5 maths starts at 607, but the average Chinese kid scores 612, a level considered elite in the rest of the world.
clips.source_hint: Anon posts about OECD PISA showing Chinese students far ahead globally
clips.text_en_b2: The latest OECD PISA report, covering 760,000 students across 91 countries, shows global math and reading scores plummeting almost everywhere. China, however, is pulling further ahead while the rest declines. The Level 5 maths threshold sits at 607, yet the average Chinese student scores 612, which puts them firmly in elite territory by international standards and leaves Hong Kong trailing badly.
clips.text_en_c1: The latest OECD PISA assessment, surveying roughly 760,000 students across 91 participating countries, paints a bleak picture of global educational outcomes, with both mathematical literacy and reading comprehension in steep, broadly synchronised decline. Against that backdrop, China's performance stands as a striking outlier. The threshold for elite Level 5 mathematical proficiency sits at 607, yet the average Chinese student now posts 612, a margin that, in practical terms, places the typical mainland pupil above the elite cut-off applied to the rest of the world's cohort. Hong Kong students, by comparison, find themselves decisively outclassed.
clips.text_en_c2: The latest OECD PISA assessment, encompassing some 760,000 students drawn from ninety-one participating nations, delivers a disquieting verdict on the global trajectory of educational attainment. Mathematics and reading scores across the developed world have plummeted precipitously, with each successive cohort seemingly less equipped than its predecessor, save for one conspicuous outlier. Chinese students have not merely weathered the decline; they have decisively outpaced every competitor, posting results that border on the preternatural. Consider that the threshold for the elite Level 5 mathematics proficiency begins at 607 points, yet the average Chinese student now registers 612, a figure that would constitute exceptional achievement almost anywhere else. Hong Kong pupils, once regional pacesetters, find themselves increasingly outflanked by their mainland counterparts. The chasm is no longer merely statistical; it portends something far more consequential for decades hence.

clips.text_zh: 暴雪班打工仔贏咗歷史性嘅工會合約，可能會定立新標準。S15啱啱睇完LCK，但呢單工會新聞對成個gaming行業更加重要。AI再勁都唔可以食晒晒。👍
clips.text_en_b1: Blizzard workers just won a historic union contract that could set a new standard for game developers. This came up on /v/ as proof the studio is 'back' under the union deal. With AI threatening every studio pipeline, organised labour inside game companies is starting to fight back against being replaced outright.
clips.source_hint: Anon celebrates Blizzard union contract as win for devs against AI
clips.text_en_b2: Blizzard's workforce has just secured a landmark union contract that could set a powerful precedent across the entire gaming industry. While competitive League streams like LCK S15 tend to dominate conversation on /v/, this labour victory arguably matters far more for the long term. With AI creeping into every production pipeline, organised workers inside studios are finally fighting back against being sidelined.
clips.text_en_c1: Blizzard's workforce has secured what can only be described as a landmark union contract, one whose ripple effects across the broader games industry could prove genuinely precedent-setting. Coming hot on the heels of S15 LCK coverage, the news lands with considerably more weight, suggesting that organised labour within major studios is finally finding its footing. With AI-driven automation threatening every stage of the development pipeline, from concept art to QA, the calculus for employees has shifted decisively. Workers are no longer content to be treated as a disposable line item awaiting algorithmic replacement, and the unionisation drive reflects precisely that sentiment.
clips.text_en_c2: In what may well prove a watershed moment for labour relations across the gaming industry, Blizzard's workforce has secured a landmark union contract whose ripple effects are likely to reverberate far beyond the studio's own corridors. Although the broader gaming discourse remains preoccupied with competitive fixtures such as the recently concluded LCK Summer Split, it is arguably this organising victory that carries the more profound long-term significance. With artificial intelligence poised to disintermediate virtually every production pipeline, from asset generation to quality assurance, the proposition that creative labour can simply be automated into obsolescence grows ever more plausible. What Blizzard's workers have demonstrated, however, is that collective bargaining retains meaningful traction even against such headwinds.

clips.text_zh: 條post話squat根本係meme lift，現代gym過度神化佢。古希臘人唔做squat嘅，佢哋跑步練腿、舉重練上身、搬重物練腿。最佳運動員就係bench、OHP、DL加跑山同搬重物。下次肥仔信再笑我squat太差我就有稿啦lol。
clips.text_en_b1: Squats are a meme lift that modern lifting over-prioritises. The ancient Greeks never did squats. They ran to train legs, lifted heavy things to train the upper body, and carried heavy loads for legs. If you want to train like the best athletes in history, all you need is bench, overhead press, deadlift, running, and carrying heavy things. Heavy squats are not required.
clips.source_hint: Anon argues squats are over-rated compared to carries and running
clips.text_en_b2: The argument basically claims squats are an overhyped meme lift that modern gym culture puts on a pedestal. Ancient Greek athletes never touched a barbell squat; they ran to build leg endurance, pressed weights overhead for upper-body strength, and hauled heavy loads to develop functional leg power. Bench, overhead press, deadlift, hill sprints, and loaded carries were more than enough.
clips.text_en_c1: The post argues, with a certain contrarian flair, that the squat has been grotesquely over-mythologised by contemporary gym culture to the point of becoming little more than a meme lift. Notably, the ancient Greeks, widely regarded as among the most functionally capable athletes in recorded history, apparently never performed them. Their conditioning came from running for leg endurance, heavy upper-body lifting for pressing strength, and hauling substantial loads for posterior chain development. If you're genuinely inclined to train like the finest athletes of antiquity, the template would be bench, overhead press, deadlift, hill running, and loaded carries. Heavy back squats, it turns out, were never strictly necessary.
clips.text_en_c2: There exists a rather seductive contrarian argument circulating within lifting communities that the squat, that most venerated of barbell exercises, is essentially a meme load that contemporary gyms have elevated to unwarranted mythological status. The historical justification, such as it is, rests upon the observation that the ancient Greeks, hardly slouches when it came to physical culture, evidently never performed anything resembling a modern bilateral squat. Their methodology instead favoured locomotion: distance running for lower body development, overhead stone work for the upper body, and the carrying of substantial loads for functional leg strength. Should one wish to train along genuinely time-honoured lines, the prescription reduces to a handful of movements: the bench press, overhead press, and deadlift for upper tension and posterior chain development, supplemented by hill running and loaded carries.

clips.text_zh: 石黑正數自己排最鍾意嘅角色、畫泳裝版，仲講咗一大堆random嘢。佢話蝦醬原型係佢小學初戀lol。Kon-senpai冇份但SD版有，廚到暹。👍
clips.text_en_b1: Ishiguro ranked his favourite characters from his own manga Soremachi, drew them in swimsuits, and talked about random stuff. Ebi-chan is based on his first crush from elementary school. Kon-senpai is missing from the list but her SD version from the gag manga is there instead.
clips.source_hint: Anon posts Ishiguro interview about Soremachi characters and his first crush
clips.text_en_b2: Ishiguro Masakazu ranked his personal favourite characters from his own manga Soremachi and even sketched them in swimsuits, chatting through a bunch of miscellaneous topics along the way. He casually dropped that Ebi-chan was essentially modelled on his elementary school crush, which is endearingly embarrassing. Kon-senpai missed the main ranking, although her SD counterpart from the gag spinoff made the cut.
clips.text_en_c1: Ishiguro Masakazu took it upon himself to rank his own favourite characters from Soremachi, commission swimsuit renditions, and meander through a characteristically tangential discourse on assorted trivia. In a disclosure that nobody particularly asked for, he revealed that Ebi-chan's design was apparently inspired by his elementary school crush, which is precisely the kind of detail one neither requires nor can successfully unlearn. Curiously absent from his rankings is Kon-senpai, though her super-deformed incarnation from the gag spin-off does receive an honourable mention. The man is, by any objective measure, a grade-A evangelist for his own creation, and longtime readers are quietly suffering for it.
clips.text_en_c2: Ishiguro Masakazu, the reclusive auteur behind the quietly beloved Soremachi, recently convened one of those disarmingly candid creator sessions in which he discoursed at length upon his own creations. The proceedings, typically equal parts shilling and confession, saw him ranking his personal favourites among the ensemble cast before sketching them in various states of beachwear, a ritual as inevitable as it is commercially motivated. Amid the expected ephemera, however, emerged a genuinely arresting revelation: the character Ebi-chan, ostensibly modelled upon a childhood acquaintance, was in fact drawn from his very first elementary school crush, a disclosure that recontextualises her rather pointed mannerisms entirely. Curiously absent from the rankings was Kon-senpai, whose conspicuous omission is partially offset by the inclusion of her super-deformed incarnation from the satirical spinoff.
